statement.essentials: Temporary weakness of part of the face is fairly common after parotid surgery and usually recovers; lasting weakness is much less common. The risk is higher with more extensive surgery, older age, a cancer, a repeat operation and a tumour in the deep part of the gland.
statement.anatomy: Weakness shows in the part of the face supplied by the affected branch. In one series lasting weakness mainly affected the marginal mandibular branch, but 10 of its 13 cases also had a neck dissection.
statement.clinical: A 2019 series of 794 parotidectomies with CT, nerve monitoring and magnification reported temporary weakness in 9.2% and permanent weakness (over 6 months) in 5.2%; old age, malignancy, recurrent tumours and tumours involving both lobes were independent risk factors, tumour size was not. A 1997 series of 259 parotidectomies found early weakness in 29% when the nerve was preserved, 16.5% after limited superficial parotidectomy for benign superficial tumours, and recovery within 6 months in 68%. A 2024 single-centre series of 160 benign parotidectomies reported 3.75% facial nerve palsy and no total paralysis.

limitations: Single-centre, mostly retrospective series with different definitions of weakness, populations (benign only, or benign and malignant) and follow-up, so the rates cannot be combined or compared with one another. The 1997 permanent-weakness figure (5.6%) is not shown because 10 of its 13 cases had a simultaneous neck dissection. The Jin abstract cites a range of 14 to 65% for immediate weakness in the literature.
disagreement: Rates of weakness differ several-fold between series, from 3.75% in a recent benign-only series to 29% early weakness in the older series; the studies do not agree on one number.
